chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Azraq from Muhammad ibn 'Isa from Abu 'Ali ibn Rashid said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), saying: 'May I be your ransom, I bought a piece of land next to my estate for two thousand dirhams. When I had paid the money, I was informed that the land was a waqf (endowment).' He said: 'The purchase of a waqf is not valid, and do not include the produce in your ownership; give it to whom it was endowed for.' I said: 'I do not know its owner.' He said: 'Give its produce in charity.'

And this report does not contradict what was narrated: Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Sahl ibn Ziyad together, and al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said: 'I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) that so-and-so bought an estate and endowed it, and allocated the khums for you in the endowment. He asks for your opinion regarding the sale of your share of the land, or valuing it for himself at the price he bought it for, or leaving it endowed.' He (peace be upon him) wrote to me: 'Inform so-and-that I command him to sell my share of the estate and deliver its price to me, and that is my opinion, if God wills; or he should value it for himself if that is more suitable for him.'

And I wrote to him that the man wrote that among those to whom the rest of this estate was endowed, there is severe disagreement, and he does not fear that this will escalate between them after him. If you think he should sell this endowment and give to each person from them what was endowed for him, command him. He wrote by his hand to me: 'And inform him that my opinion for him, if he has known the disagreement among the owners of the endowment, is that selling the endowment is better, for perhaps in the disagreement there will be loss of wealth and lives.'

Because the principle in endowments is that their sale is not valid, according to what the first report contained. The last report came only as a concession based on what it contained, which is that being an endowment leads to harm, disagreement, confusion, and destruction of the endowment. Therefore, at that time, its sale is valid and giving each person with a right their right. That which is valid to be sold is valid only for the owners of the endowment, not for others. The first report does not state that the one who sold it was the one it was endowed for; rather, it is apparent from it that the one who sold it was someone not connected to it, therefore its sale was not valid. And that which clarifies what we mentioned regarding the prohibition of the validity of selling the endowment is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: Can a waqf (Islamic endowment) be sold according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of *waqf* (endowment), establishing the general principle that *waqf* property is inalienable and its produce belongs to the endowed cause. However, it introduces a critical exception based on *darar* (harm) and *ikhtilaf* (disagreement), allowing for the sale of the endowment to prevent the loss of wealth or life among co-owners, a ruling attributed to Imam al-Sadiq (AS). This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the underlying wisdom (*hikmah*) of preservation over rigid formalism when disputes threaten the utility of the endowment.
